node.label: Jennifer L. Morgan
node.date_label: “Some Could Suckle over Their Shoulder” (1997) · Laboring Women (2004) · Connexions, co-editor (2016) · “Partus sequitur ventrem” (2018) · Reckoning with Slavery (2021)
node.description: In Laboring Women (2004), Jennifer L. Morgan argues that enslaved women’s agricultural work and capacity to bear children jointly shaped racial slavery in the English Atlantic. Reckoning with Slavery (2021) extends that inquiry by treating race, kinship and numerical valuations as mutually constitutive: enslavers denied African kinship while exploiting maternal descent to reproduce their property. Morgan reads enslaved women as people who understood and contested these transformations, and treats the omissions in commercial and legal records as part of the history to be explained. Hartman subsequently drew on Morgan’s maternity argument in “The Belly of the World” (2016).
node.representative_figures_and_works: “Some Could Suckle over Their Shoulder” (1997); Laboring Women: Reproduction and Gender in New World Slavery (2004); Connexions: Histories of Race and Sex in North America (2016), co-edited with Jennifer Brier and Jim Downs; “Partus sequitur ventrem” (2018); Reckoning with Slavery: Gender, Kinship, and Capitalism in the Early Black Atlantic (2021).
node.scope_note: Selected passages in the publisher’s Reckoning with Slavery preview, including acknowledgments xi–xiii and the introduction, were read; the chapters and conclusion remain unread. Laboring Women is characterised from the MacArthur Foundation’s 2024 citation and Hartman’s 2016 note, not its body. “Partus sequitur ventrem” (2018) is listed bibliographically; its body is unread. Hartman’s essay was read in an authorized institutional reprint; its journal facsimile and Morgan’s 2014 workshop remain unread. Other selected publications were checked bibliographically; cited predecessors’ complete works were not freshly read.

proposed_edges.relationship: In the acknowledgments to Reckoning with Slavery (2021), Morgan credits Deborah Gray White’s pioneering scholarship and critical support as foundations for her own work.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Acknowledgments p. xi, last sentences of first paragraph: “trailblazing” work and critical support. This is Morgan’s explicit intellectual acknowledgment, not an inferred employer link; no particular White title is specified here and none is silently supplied. White’s books unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Reckoning with Slavery (2021), Morgan names Hartman's work among the scholarship that shaped the book and that she strives to emulate, and notes that her use of 'political arithmetic' echoes Hartman's Lose Your Mother (2007).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction p. 13 n. 28 explicitly discusses Hartman’s phrase “political arithmetic” and its earlier demographic meaning. Acknowledgments p. xiii and p. 11 n. 22 corroborate a broader debt. This claim concerns the specified use, not adoption of every element of critical fabulation. Hartman’s book unread; her 2007 original date is distinguished from the 2008 edition named in Morgan’s epigraph.
proposed_edges.map_label: Hartman's work as model; political arithmetic

proposed_edges.relationship: In Reckoning with Slavery (2021), Morgan names Johnson’s “To Remake the World” as a resource for understanding slavery and capitalism together.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction p. 16 n. 33 calls Johnson’s formulation “generative”; pp. 15–16 place the book beside scholars developing Robinson’s work. Specific methodological resource, not a claim of coauthorship or sole derivation. Johnson’s essay itself unread; conflicting secondary dates were not promoted to an original publication date.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Reckoning with Slavery (2021), Morgan places her account of gender, kinship and capitalism in dialogue with scholarship returning to Williams’s Capitalism and Slavery (1944).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction p. 11: “starting point”; pp. 16–17 and n. 33 state dialogue with renewed Williams scholarship. Morgan extends a research programme through reproductive labor and cultural logic; she does not here endorse every Williams claim about abolition. Williams’s original book not freshly read; 1944 matches the inspected existing Williams node.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Reckoning with Slavery (2021), Morgan criticizes The Order of Things for omitting African experiences from its account of early modern knowledge.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction p. 13 n. 29, following discussion of the shift from display to tables: “experienced by Africans”; p. 18 n. 37 adds the contrast with Trouillot. A specific criticism of this book’s analytic omission, not rejection of Foucault’s entire scholarship. Foucault’s original and translation unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Reckoning with Slavery (2021), Morgan names Trouillot among the scholars whose work shaped the book, and sets his account of the unthinkable in Silencing the Past against Foucault.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Printed p. 17, final paragraph and n. 58 explicitly identify an “obvious debt” to Trouillot. The claim concerns this formulation about archival absence and strategic thought. Morgan’s note dates the cited book 1992; the existing graph records original 1995, so the note’s date is not repeated as publication fact. Trouillot’s book not freshly read.

proposed_edges.relationship: Morgan’s acknowledgments to Reckoning with Slavery (2021) identify Burton’s repeated manuscript readings and help in conceptualizing and completing the book.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Acknowledgments p. xii, paragraph on readers of multiple drafts: “conceptualizing” identifies substantive project help. Burton is singled out as reading each draft; this is specified intellectual work, not generic thanks or institutional proximity. No independent account by Burton of those readings consulted.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Reckoning with Slavery (2021), Morgan uses Sontag’s Regarding the Pain of Others to ask how commercial records neutralize the suffering behind slave-trade numbers.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction p. 20 and n. 40: Morgan introduces Sontag through “wrath” and applies the point to ledgers and inventories; p. 21 develops the application. Limited borrowing for a representational problem; Sontag’s book unread and no wholesale theoretical allegiance inferred.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The Belly of the World” (2016), Hartman uses Morgan’s work on maternity and slave law to explain the reproductive foundations of racial slavery.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Authorized 2017 HTML reprint, paragraph beginning Kinship loses meaning: “Extending and revising”; notes 1 and 7. Note 1 explicitly discusses Laboring Women (2004); note 7 points to a 2014 Irvine workshop called Partus Sequitur Ventrem. The later published 2018 article was not Hartman’s 2016 source. Original journal facsimile and workshop unread; this distinct incoming debt is not the reverse projection of Morgan’s 2021 Hartman citation.
proposed_edges.map_label: Hartman draws on Morgan’s maternity argument

proposed_edges.relationship: Laboring Women (2004) makes enslaved women’s work and childbearing central to the history of colonial slavery.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: MacArthur Foundation, Jennifer L. Morgan (1 October 2024), About Jennifer’s Work, paragraph beginning Morgan wrote her groundbreaking first book, read on the Foundation’s own site. The paragraph identifies Laboring Women (2004) and explains its account of agricultural labor and childbearing under slavery. This is institutional reception of the book, not an independent reading of the monograph. The edge is now supported by this single read source.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Reckoning with Slavery (2021), Morgan argues that Virginia's 1662 rule that a child's condition followed the mother's tethered enslaved women's reproduction to enslavement, making racial slavery heritable and denying enslaved people kinship.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Jennifer L. Morgan, Reckoning with Slavery (Duke University Press, 2021), publisher preview, introduction Refusing Demography, printed pp. 3–5 (PDF leaves 19–21), read. Printed pp. 3–4 discuss the 1662 maternal-status rule; p. 5 links hereditary enslavement, reproduction, property rights and the denial of kinship. These are passages from the book’s introduction, not selected article pages. The full book and the underlying legal records were not independently read.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Reckoning with Slavery (2021), Morgan connects women’s commodification across Iberia, West Africa, the Middle Passage, the Caribbean and mainland colonies.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction pp. 26–27, especially the explicit geographic arc and proposal to center enslaved women over “geographies”; pp. 3–5 explain kinship and commodification. This is a stated Atlantic research design and argument, not shared-topic membership. Chapter bodies unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Women and kinship across the Atlantic

proposed_edges.relationship: In Reckoning with Slavery (2021), Morgan argues that reproductive dispossession, race and numerical valuations developed together in early Atlantic capitalism.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction pp. 15–17, especially p. 16 and n. 31, state the intervention through “reproduction”; pp. 10–11 explain relatedness. This concerns the constitutive logic of racial capitalism; not an estimate of slavery’s numerical contribution to industrial growth. Full monograph beyond introduction unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Gender and kinship in racial capitalism

proposed_edges.relationship: Discussing the research behind Dispossessed Lives (2016), Marisa J. Fuentes says that reading Jennifer Morgan’s social histories of enslaved women shaped her expectation of finding fuller accounts of their lives in Barbados’s archives.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Fuentes’s answers in Andrew Mitchell Davenport’s 8 March 2017 interview. She directly connects her reading of Morgan and Beckles to her initial research expectations, then explains how archival absences changed her project. This establishes a particular influence on research expectations, not adoption of Morgan’s entire argument. The interview does not identify the Morgan title; the dated work named in the relationship is Fuentes’s 2016 book. The interview’s spelling of Beckles’s name is retained only in the verbatim phrase. Source record gb162_fuentes_davenport_2017 already exists in the graph and was freshly checked.
proposed_edges.map_label: Social histories shaped Fuentes’s archival expectations

proposed_edges.relationship: In Reckoning with Slavery (2021), Morgan proposes reading surviving evidence of enslaved women together with the ideologies that produced their archival absence.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read selected introduction passages in Duke University Press’s licensed preview, reached through the publisher’s book page and its introduction link. On pp. 9–10 Morgan examines how records erase and enumerate; p. 24 explicitly states the proposed method. The edge records a contribution to studying archival production, not complete recovery of missing lives. The full book and the chapters summarized by the introduction remain unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Explains the production of archival absence

proposed_edges.relationship: As Erika Denise Edwards explains in her 2022 review essay, Morgan’s Reckoning with Slavery (2021) examines how racial categories and numerical valuation developed through the commodification of African women in the Atlantic slave trade.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the opening discussion and Morgan-specific paragraphs of Edwards’s open review essay on Cambridge Core. This edge concerns historical racial formation, without asserting membership in any particular theoretical school. Edwards is not an eligible person endpoint, so her review supplies evidence for a field contribution rather than a reviewer–author edge.
proposed_edges.map_label: Numeracy and the formation of racial categories
